evidence.text: The sun

evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[2]
evidence.text: 實也。太陽之精不虧。从囗一。象形。凡日之屬皆从日。

evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[3]
evidence.text:
Characters in the same phonetic series (日) (Zhengzhang, 2003)
Pictogram (象形) – the sun. A dot or line was added in the centre to distinguish it from visually similar characters, e.g. 囗 (early form of 丁). Compare earlier forms of the character with the astronomical and astrological symbol for the Sun (☉) and the Egyptian hieroglyph 𓇳.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ku-ni(k). Cognate to Tibetan ཉི་མ (nyi ma, “sun, day”), Burmese နေ (ne, “sun”) or Burmese နေ့ (ne., “day”), S'gaw Karen နံၤ (nĩ, “day”), and Nuosu ꑍ (nyip, “day, daytime”).

evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[4]
evidence.text: Essentially a substitute character for 入 (MC nyip, “to enter”) that preserves the expected modern pronunciation of 入; see the etymology there for more.

evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[5]
evidence.text: Possibly due to assimilation of 金 (kim) and 日 (nyit). Note that 金 ends with /m/ in Old and Middle Chinese.

evidence.source: Multi-function Chinese Character Database, Academia Sinica
evidence.field: Oracle-bone character entry; paleographic account and cited inscriptions
evidence.text: The database describes 日 as a depiction of the sun, with early round forms sometimes squared because a circle was difficult to carve on bone; it says the central mark distinguished the graph from 囗. It cites Shang oracle-bone examples for the sun and sunrise (合集34163), eclipse (合集11480), daylight contrasted with evening (合集33871, 合集34036), and a period of five days (合集12314). It also notes later bronze-inscription uses for the sun, daylight, and calendar-day unit. The inscription citations substantiate distinct early uses; they do not by themselves establish the order in which those senses developed.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：日

evidence.field: Character evolution page
evidence.text: The entry provides examples under oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscripts, seal script, and Shuowen headings, and states that 日 resembles the sun and its original meaning is the sun. The page identifies a bronze example as inscription 集成05990. Its displayed categories support a broad sequence of attested script traditions, but the accessible text does not supply dates for each individual form.
evidence.title: 漢字「日」：字形演變

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, digitized 說文解字 with 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.field: 卷七 日部 entry and commentary
evidence.text: Xu Shen's entry defines 日 as 實, describes it as 太陽之精不虧, analyzes it as 从囗一 and calls it pictographic. Duan Yucai explains the outer shape as the sun's outline and the inner stroke as its undiminished center. This is the received Han-era account, not direct evidence for the graph's earliest form; the oracle-bone material provides earlier evidence.
evidence.title: 說文解字「日」

evidence.field: 形義通解: glyph account and oracle-bone citations
evidence.text: The entry explains that 日 depicts the sun, with early round forms sometimes rendered square because circles were difficult to carve on bone; it says the central mark distinguished 日 from 囗. context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.
